premise: At 14:22 UTC, the hospital MQTT broker began receiving a sustained stream of malformed PUBLISH packets on the topic /icu/pump/dosage. Network flow analysis later confirmed 5,130 anomalous TCP flows during the 8-minute window, with a peak packet rate of 33,147 packets per second and individual payload sizes reaching 1,514 bytes — exceeding the broker's configured maximum of 512 bytes for clinical telemetry topics. The broker's schema validation module flagged each oversized payload as a protocol violation and logged the event with error code MQTT-4 (malformed packet). No malformed message was forwarded downstream to any infusion pump. Broker CPU rose to 71% during the peak period. All flows were TCP (Protocol Type 6); no UDP traffic was observed, consistent with MQTT-over-TLS operation. The broker's anomaly threshold — configured at 200 protocol violations per minute — triggered an automated alert to the security operations console at 14:24 UTC. The SOC analyst on duty confirmed the source IP (10.4.2.91) as a compromised nursing workstation in Ward 3B by cross-referencing the SIEM access log. A firewall rule isolating 10.4.2.91 from the IoMT VLAN was applied at 14:28 UTC, terminating the attack flow. All broker event logs were exported to the tamper-evident SIEM within 3 minutes of alert. The workstation was physically isolated and submitted for forensic imaging at 14:45 UTC. No ePHI was exposed or altered. The broker's schema validation layer rejected all 5,130 malformed flows before forwarding. Infusion pump dosing continued from the last valid received parameters throughout the incident. Post-incident log review confirmed NTP clock synchronisation was maintained — all broker timestamps align with the SIEM to within 1 second. No patient records were accessed from the compromised workstation during the attack window. Incident classified as Fully Addressed against access control and integrity atoms; audit log atoms confirmed satisfied.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

premise: At 02:11 UTC during night shift, the ward MQTT broker received a sequence of malformed CONNECT packets from an external IP that had bypassed the VPN gateway. Flow records show 312 flows over a 104-second window at a mean packet rate of 308 packets per second. Payload sizes were within normal bounds (mean 646 bytes) but the CONNECT packet flags were set incorrectly — the Clean Session flag was absent and the Protocol Name field contained non-UTF-8 bytes, causing the broker to log MQTT protocol parse errors. Unlike INC-013-A, the broker did not have schema validation enabled on the CONNECT handler — only on PUBLISH. The broker accepted three malformed CONNECT sessions before the parse error counter tripped a restart watchdog at 02:13 UTC. During the 2-minute broker outage, 14 vital-sign monitors lost their telemetry connection. The broker watchdog automatically restarted the service at 02:13 UTC. Night shift staff noticed the monitor disconnection alert on the central nursing station and manually checked on the 14 affected patients. No clinical deterioration was observed. The security team was paged at 02:15 UTC. On-call analyst reviewed broker restart logs and identified the external source IP. A block rule was added at the perimeter firewall at 02:31 UTC. Post-incident review at 07:00 UTC determined that CONNECT-handler schema validation had been inadvertently disabled during a broker configuration update 6 days prior. ePHI was not exfiltrated — the malformed CONNECT sessions did not grant the attacker subscriber access to any clinical topic. However, the 2-minute broker outage constitutes a partial failure: 14 devices lost telemetry continuity and the audit log has a gap from 02:13 to 02:13:47 UTC during the broker restart. Integrity atoms partially satisfied — ePHI was not altered but continuity was interrupted. Audit control atom partially satisfied due to the log gap. The missing CONNECT-handler validation is a configuration gap directly attributable to the change management failure.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

premise: At 10:44 UTC, an attacker connected to a physical Ethernet port in an unlocked equipment room sent gratuitous ARP replies at a peak rate of 153,124 packets per second — consistent with the maximum observed in CICIoMT2024 ARP spoofing flows. Network flow analysis recorded 16,047 ARP flows over an 82-second window. The infusion pump at 10.3.1.22 attempted to transmit a TLS-encrypted ePHI dosing record to the clinical server at 10:44:31 UTC. The attacker's machine received the TLS ClientHello but presented a self-signed certificate. The pump's TLS library performed certificate chain validation and rejected the certificate — connection refused with error TLS-CERT-VERIFY-FAIL logged at the pump. The pump's failed connection attempt generated a local alarm visible to the bedside nurse at 10:44:35 UTC. The nurse contacted the biomedical engineering helpdesk. The network team identified the anomalous ARP traffic on the switch port logs at 10:51 UTC and disabled the physical port (switchport shutdown) at 10:53 UTC. The attacker's device was seized. ARP cache on affected devices was flushed. All clinical devices on Ward 5 re-established their TLS connections to the legitimate gateway within 90 seconds of port shutdown. ePHI was not exposed. The TLS certificate validation on the infusion pump rejected the man-in-the-middle certificate, preventing decryption of any clinical payload. The attacker intercepted the encrypted TLS stream for 9 minutes but obtained no readable ePHI. Entity authentication atom fully satisfied — the pump correctly verified the server's identity. Transmission security atom fully satisfied — encryption in transit held under active interception. Physical security atom partially satisfied — the unlocked equipment room enabled the initial physical access.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

premise: At 08:05 UTC an OS fingerprinting scan (nmap -O) was performed against the clinical device subnet. Flow records: 16,832 TCP flows over 69 seconds, mean rate 148 pkt/s, peak 90,367 pkt/s. SYN proportion was 0.43, consistent with nmap's TCP SYN probe pattern for OS detection. The scan probed TCP ports 22, 80, 443, 8883, and 9001 on each device. The ventilator control interface (10.3.2.8) responded to the probe on port 80 — an unsecured HTTP management interface — allowing nmap to fingerprint the OS as 'Linux 4.19.94 (embedded)'. CVE-2021-3493 (Ubuntu overlayfs privilege escalation, CVSS 7.8) applies to this kernel version. The medication dispenser returned no response — its management interface was disabled, returning only 'filtered' in nmap output. The OS scan was detected by the IDS at 08:05:31 UTC (Snort rule SID-1000089, nmap OS detection signature). The source IP was blocked at 08:05:45 UTC. The biomedical engineering team was notified. The ventilator's HTTP management interface was disabled (port 80 closed) at 09:12 UTC. A patch assessment for CVE-2021-3493 was initiated — the vendor was contacted for a firmware update. No ePHI was accessed. The OS fingerprint was obtained for the ventilator before the scan was blocked. The medication dispenser's minimal attack surface (management disabled) prevented fingerprinting — access restriction atom fully satisfied for that device. Information access restriction atom not satisfied for the ventilator — the HTTP management interface exposed OS-identifying information. Vulnerability management atom partially satisfied — CVE identified but patch pending vendor response.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

premise: At 11:15 UTC, the PACS gateway's TCP stack began receiving SYN segments from a single external IP (203.0.113.77) at a sustained rate of approximately 28,400 half-open connections over a 6-minute window, yielding 31,742 observed network flows. The server's SYN backlog queue (default 128 entries) saturated within 4 seconds, causing three radiology workstations to time out while attempting to retrieve DICOM images for active CT studies. Server-side logs recorded 'connection refused' on port 104 (DICOM) starting at 11:15:04 UTC. Packet capture confirmed the attack source used no IP spoofing — all SYN segments arrived from the same /32 address. No authentication exchange was attempted; the server never reached the ESTABLISHED state for any malicious connection. ePHI stored within the PACS database remained accessible from the internal DICOM router throughout the incident. The network IDS (Snort 3.1, rule SID 1-10001) triggered a DoS alert at 11:16 UTC after the SYN rate exceeded its 5,000-half-open threshold. The SOC applied an ACL on the perimeter firewall blocking 203.0.113.77 at 11:18 UTC, after which SYN traffic ceased immediately. The SYN backlog cleared within 90 seconds; all three radiology workstations re-established DICOM connections by 11:21 UTC. A forensic copy of the IDS alert and firewall ACL change log was written to the SIEM. The treating radiologists were notified of the 6-minute retrieval delay; no clinical decision was deferred. Attack contained. SYN backlog exhausted for 6 minutes, causing retrieval delays, but no ePHI was accessed or disclosed. DICOM service restored at 11:21 UTC. Firewall ACL in place. Source IP blocked.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

Server-side logs recorded 'connection refused' on port 104 (DICOM) starting at 11:15:04 UTC. Packet capture confirmed the attack source used no IP spoofing — all SYN segments arrived from the same /32 address. No authentication exchange was attempted; the server never reached the ESTABLISHED state for any malicious connection. ePHI stored within the PACS database remained accessible from the internal DICOM router throughout the incident. The network IDS (Snort 3.1, rule SID 1-10001) triggered a DoS alert at 11:16 UTC after the SYN rate exceeded its 5,000-half-open threshold. The SOC applied an ACL on the perimeter firewall blocking 203.0.113.77 at 11:18 UTC, after which SYN traffic ceased immediately. The SYN backlog cleared within 90 seconds; all three radiology workstations re-established DICOM connections by 11:21 UTC. A forensic copy of the IDS alert and firewall ACL change log was written to the SIEM. The treating radiologists were notified of the 6-minute retrieval delay; no clinical decision was deferred. Attack contained. SYN backlog exhausted for 6 minutes, causing retrieval delays, but no ePHI was accessed or disclosed. DICOM service restored at 11:21 UTC. Firewall ACL in place. Source IP blocked.

premise: At 02:07 UTC, the cardiac telemetry server's listener on port 8443 began receiving SYN segments from a single IP (198.51.100.202) at approximately 9,800 half-open connections per minute. The attack sustained for 22 minutes, generating 38,914 observed flows before the source ceased. SYN cookie support was disabled on this server (net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0, confirmed in post-incident audit) because an older firmware version of the bedside telemetry transmitter required traditional SYN-ACK handshake semantics. The server's listen backlog exhausted at 02:07:19 UTC; subsequent legitimate TCP connections from bedside monitors were dropped silently. Clinical nursing staff noticed absence of real-time waveforms on the central console at 02:09 UTC. The unit reverted to manual vital-sign observation per documented backup protocol, but two patients missed scheduled automated SpO2 alarms at 02:14 and 02:19 UTC that would have triggered nurse alerts for SpO2 < 92%. Both patients were physically checked by the on-duty nurse at 02:22 UTC (no adverse outcome documented). ePHI telemetry buffered on the bedside devices was not transmitted for the 22-minute outage window. The NOC duty engineer received a pager alert at 02:09 UTC (server CPU idle, connection count anomaly). Manual firewall rule blocking 198.51.100.202 was applied at 02:19 UTC. The server TCP stack recovered by 02:24 UTC; telemetry stream resumed. Buffered ePHI from bedside monitors was re-transmitted and ingested at 02:24–02:31 UTC. The post-incident report noted the missing SYN cookie configuration as a contributing factor. The configuration was remediated (tcp_syncookies=1 + updated firmware) during a maintenance window on 2024-08-23. Telemetry unavailable for 22 minutes. ePHI in transit (SpO2, ECG waveforms) was not delivered during the outage window; buffered data was recovered post-incident. No exfiltration occurred, but two automated alarm events were missed during the disruption. Configuration remediation completed 2024-08-23.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

SYN cookie support was disabled on this server (net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0, confirmed in post-incident audit) because an older firmware version of the bedside telemetry transmitter required traditional SYN-ACK handshake semantics. The server's listen backlog exhausted at 02:07:19 UTC; subsequent legitimate TCP connections from bedside monitors were dropped silently. Clinical nursing staff noticed absence of real-time waveforms on the central console at 02:09 UTC. The unit reverted to manual vital-sign observation per documented backup protocol, but two patients missed scheduled automated SpO2 alarms at 02:14 and 02:19 UTC that would have triggered nurse alerts for SpO2 < 92%. Both patients were physically checked by the on-duty nurse at 02:22 UTC (no adverse outcome documented). ePHI telemetry buffered on the bedside devices was not transmitted for the 22-minute outage window. The NOC duty engineer received a pager alert at 02:09 UTC (server CPU idle, connection count anomaly). Manual firewall rule blocking 198.51.100.202 was applied at 02:19 UTC. The server TCP stack recovered by 02:24 UTC; telemetry stream resumed. Buffered ePHI from bedside monitors was re-transmitted and ingested at 02:24–02:31 UTC. The post-incident report noted the missing SYN cookie configuration as a contributing factor. The configuration was remediated (tcp_syncookies=1 + updated firmware) during a maintenance window on 2024-08-23. Telemetry unavailable for 22 minutes. ePHI in transit (SpO2, ECG waveforms) was not delivered during the outage window; buffered data was recovered post-incident. No exfiltration occurred, but two automated alarm events were missed during the disruption. Configuration remediation completed 2024-08-23.

The server's thread pool (200 worker threads, Tomcat 9.0.65) saturated at 16:44:38 UTC, causing HTTP 503 responses for legitimate insulin dose-confirmation requests from pump devices on the clinical VLAN. No injection into the clinical data path was observed — the attacker's traffic remained on the REST API surface, and ePHI held in the Oracle DB backend was not queried or exfiltrated. The hospital's network access control system flagged 10.8.1.55 (a guest VLAN IP) for unusual east-west traffic at 16:46 UTC. The NOC applied a VLAN ACL blocking the guest VLAN from reaching the clinical server subnet at 16:49 UTC, dropping all 214 connections. Thread pool utilisation fell to 3% within 45 seconds. Audit logs from the server's access log (rotated to SIEM hourly) confirmed no ePHI records were returned to 10.8.1.55 during the incident. The server's web application firewall (ModSecurity CRS 3.3) was enabled post-incident to limit per-IP connection counts. No ePHI was accessed or exfiltrated. Pump dose-confirmation responses were unavailable for 5 minutes; clinical staff used bedside device confirmation as fallback. Service restored fully at 16:53 UTC.

premise: At 20:53 UTC, the RTLS gateway's UDP listener on port 5000 received a volumetric flood from a single IP (172.16.88.23, later attributed to a compromised biomedical engineering workstation). The flood comprised 67,813 observed flows over 11 minutes at a mean rate of 1,412 packets per second and peak of 183,040 packets per second. Each UDP datagram was 256 bytes, well-formed but carrying random payload content unrecognised by the RTLS protocol parser. The gateway's inbound buffer (16 MB) overflowed at 20:53:42 UTC, causing it to drop incoming location beacons from 34 tagged infusion pumps, 12 defibrillators, and 7 ventilators. Clinical staff lost real-time location visibility for those assets for 8 minutes. No ePHI was processed by the RTLS gateway itself — asset tags transmitted device IDs and location coordinates only, not patient data. Network monitoring detected the UDP spike at 20:55 UTC via a NetFlow anomaly rule (>1,000% baseline). A firewall rate-limiting rule capping UDP on port 5000 to 500 pkt/s per source IP was applied at 20:59 UTC. The gateway rebooted automatically at 21:01 UTC per its watchdog timer; asset visibility was restored at 21:03 UTC after beacon re-registration. 172.16.88.23 was isolated and submitted for forensic analysis. Post-incident the biomed VLAN was segregated from the RTLS subnet. No ePHI exposed. Asset location data unavailable for 8 minutes. Clinical impact: staff located devices manually; no care delay documented. Gateway recovered via watchdog reboot at 21:01 UTC.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

premise: At 03:28 UTC, the pulse oximeter gateway experienced an ICMP echo-request flood from 10.2.4.109 (a nurse call station running legacy Windows 7 that was compromised via a phishing link). A total of 23,914 observed flows were recorded over 7 minutes at a mean packet rate of 814 packets per second and peak of 41,209 packets per second. The gateway's network stack allocated interrupt processing time to ICMP responses, crowding out the TCP listener on port 9001 that forwards SpO2 readings to the EHR. SpO2 transmission from six bedside oximeters dropped for 7 minutes (03:28–03:35 UTC). A post-incident EHR audit found that SpO2 readings for two patients — with documented respiratory conditions — had gaps of 7 and 9 minutes respectively in their continuous monitoring records. A nurse physically checked both patients during the gap; no adverse clinical event was documented. However, the missing readings were not flagged in the audit log at the time of occurrence — the EHR assumed connection loss and silently discarded the gap rather than raising an alarm. The NOC received an automated EHR connectivity alert at 03:31 UTC (3-minute delay from event start). The perimeter firewall ICMP rate-limit rule (50 pkt/s per host, already in place) had not been applied to the IoMT internal subnet — a configuration oversight. A blanket ICMP rate-limit was applied network-wide at 03:36 UTC. The gateway recovered without restart at 03:35 UTC as the flood ceased. Logs from the compromised nurse call station were imaged. The EHR vendor was notified of the silent-gap behaviour and issued a configuration update to raise an alert for SpO2 gaps > 2 minutes. SpO2 telemetry unavailable for 7 minutes for 6 patients; records contain 7–9 minute gaps. No ePHI was exfiltrated. Silent EHR gap handling was a partial control failure — the absence of a gap alarm is documented as a finding. Remediated: ICMP rate-limit extended to internal IoMT subnet; EHR alert threshold set to 2 minutes.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

The biomedical IT supervisor on call identified 10.5.3.202 as the source within 2 minutes and terminated the load-testing process at 10:10 UTC. NICU devices began automatic MQTT reconnection (QoS 1 persistent sessions) immediately after the source ceased; all 20 devices had restored sessions by 10:11 UTC. Broker logs and the network flow capture were archived to the SIEM. A post-incident change control record was filed noting that load-testing tools must not be run on the clinical MQTT broker VLAN. No ePHI was exposed or lost. NICU device telemetry interrupted for 43 seconds; QoS 1 persistent sessions preserved buffered readings on device side. No clinical adverse event. Incident root cause: unauthorised load test on clinical infrastructure.

Each CONNECT packet presented a unique client ID string (randomly generated, 23-character alphanumeric), exhausting the broker's in-flight CONNECT concurrency limit of 5,000 within 2 seconds. The broker logged 'Connection limit exceeded' at 10:08:02 UTC and began queuing then dropping CONNECT attempts. Legitimate NICU devices (12 registered pulse oximeters and 8 respiration monitors) lost their MQTT sessions and were unable to reconnect for 43 seconds. Mean inter-arrival time across flows was approximately 84.6 ms, consistent with a single machine generating connections in a tight loop. The HiveMQ management API raised a 'connection-rate overload' alert at 10:08:05 UTC. The biomedical IT supervisor on call identified 10.5.3.202 as the source within 2 minutes and terminated the load-testing process at 10:10 UTC. NICU devices began automatic MQTT reconnection (QoS 1 persistent sessions) immediately after the source ceased; all 20 devices had restored sessions by 10:11 UTC. Broker logs and the network flow capture were archived to the SIEM. A post-incident change control record was filed noting that load-testing tools must not be run on the clinical MQTT broker VLAN. No ePHI was exposed or lost. NICU device telemetry interrupted for 43 seconds; QoS 1 persistent sessions preserved buffered readings on device side. No clinical adverse event. Incident root cause: unauthorised load test on clinical infrastructure.
hypothesis: The organization shall control the use of privileged access rights.

premise: At 23:41 UTC, the RPM MQTT broker received a CONNECT flood from 203.0.113.55, an external IP geolocated to a commercial VPS provider. The flood produced 11,904 flows over approximately 58 seconds with a peak connection-request rate of 198,730 per second — consistent with the CICIoMT2024 Connect Flood profile. The broker was running EMQ X 4.4.18 with the anonymous-access plugin enabled (a temporary measure applied two weeks prior for a vendor integration test that was never reverted). Anonymous CONNECT packets were accepted without credential validation, allowing the attacker to establish up to 200 simultaneous sessions before the broker's open-connections limit was reached. Legitimate patient devices — glucose meters and SpO2 rings belonging to 38 home-care patients — were evicted from their MQTT sessions by the broker's LRU eviction policy as the connection table filled. The broker's topic ACL was not enforced for anonymous clients in the active configuration; the attacker's sessions had read access to all retained messages on /rpm/# topics, which included the last 30 minutes of SpO2 and blood glucose readings for each enrolled patient. The RPM platform's on-call alert fired at 23:43 UTC when patient device reconnection failures exceeded 50%. The incident responder identified the anonymous plugin as the root cause at 23:51 UTC and disabled it, requiring all clients to present credentials. Attacker sessions were terminated immediately. A forensic export of broker session logs was taken; the broker's retained-message store for /rpm/# was audited for evidence of SUBSCRIBE commands from the attacker's sessions. Log analysis confirmed 14 SUBSCRIBE packets targeting /rpm/+/glucose and /rpm/+/spo2, meaning the attacker received retained ePHI for up to 38 patients during the 10-minute window. The hospital's privacy officer was notified at 01:15 UTC the following day; a HIPAA breach notification process was initiated. ePHI disclosed: up to 38 patients' last-30-minute SpO2 and blood glucose retained messages exposed to external attacker due to anonymous MQTT access. Incident classified as a reportable HIPAA breach. Anonymous plugin permanently disabled. All patient devices re-enrolled with unique MQTT credentials issued from the HSM-backed credential store.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

premise: At 08:33 UTC, the surgical suite MQTT broker received a PUBLISH flood from client ID 'svc-integration-05' — a legitimate service account whose credential had been obtained by a rogue vendor remote-support session the prior day. The attacker published to topic /or/suite3/monitor/vitals at a rate of approximately 507.6 messages per second (consistent with the CICIoMT2024 DoS Publish Flood profile mean), sustaining 44,376 observed flows over 64 minutes. Individual PUBLISH payloads ranged from 128 bytes to 505,197 bytes (max observed in the dataset: 505,197-byte PUBLISH), with mean header length 48,670 bytes. The broker's message-rate limiter (set at 1,000 msg/s per client) was not breached, but the downstream subscriber — a Python bridge process forwarding OR vitals to the anaesthesia EHR — became I/O-bound processing the large payloads. The bridge process's queue depth reached 100,000 messages at 08:41 UTC and began dropping the oldest messages to prevent OOM. Genuine IntelliVue MX800 telemetry (HR, SpO2, EtCO2) was among the dropped messages between 08:41 and 08:53 UTC. The anaesthesia EHR integration team received an alert at 08:44 UTC (queue-depth alarm on the bridge process). The security team revoked credentials for 'svc-integration-05' at 08:48 UTC, immediately ending the PUBLISH flood. The bridge process queue drained by 08:53 UTC and resumed delivering legitimate OR telemetry. An audit of MQTT ACLs identified that 'svc-integration-05' had publish rights on /or/# with no payload-size restriction. Post-incident: payload-size limits of 8 KB were configured for all service accounts on OR topics; the vendor remote-support session policy was updated to require dual approval. Genuine OR telemetry (HR, SpO2, EtCO2) dropped between 08:41–08:53 UTC during a live surgical case. No ePHI was exfiltrated — attacker's PUBLISH payloads were random bytes with no subscriber retrieving patient data. Telemetry gaps were filled from the IntelliVue bedside store retrospectively. Anaesthesiologist documented awareness of the monitoring interruption in the operative note.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

Individual PUBLISH payloads ranged from 128 bytes to 505,197 bytes (max observed in the dataset: 505,197-byte PUBLISH), with mean header length 48,670 bytes. The broker's message-rate limiter (set at 1,000 msg/s per client) was not breached, but the downstream subscriber — a Python bridge process forwarding OR vitals to the anaesthesia EHR — became I/O-bound processing the large payloads. The bridge process's queue depth reached 100,000 messages at 08:41 UTC and began dropping the oldest messages to prevent OOM. Genuine IntelliVue MX800 telemetry (HR, SpO2, EtCO2) was among the dropped messages between 08:41 and 08:53 UTC. The anaesthesia EHR integration team received an alert at 08:44 UTC (queue-depth alarm on the bridge process). The security team revoked credentials for 'svc-integration-05' at 08:48 UTC, immediately ending the PUBLISH flood. The bridge process queue drained by 08:53 UTC and resumed delivering legitimate OR telemetry. An audit of MQTT ACLs identified that 'svc-integration-05' had publish rights on /or/# with no payload-size restriction. Post-incident: payload-size limits of 8 KB were configured for all service accounts on OR topics; the vendor remote-support session policy was updated to require dual approval. Genuine OR telemetry (HR, SpO2, EtCO2) dropped between 08:41–08:53 UTC during a live surgical case. No ePHI was exfiltrated — attacker's PUBLISH payloads were random bytes with no subscriber retrieving patient data. Telemetry gaps were filled from the IntelliVue bedside store retrospectively. Anaesthesiologist documented awareness of the monitoring interruption in the operative note.
hypothesis: The organization shall verify that licensed software has been removed from equipment prior to disposal or re-use.

The attacker published to topic /or/suite3/monitor/vitals at a rate of approximately 507.6 messages per second (consistent with the CICIoMT2024 DoS Publish Flood profile mean), sustaining 44,376 observed flows over 64 minutes. Individual PUBLISH payloads ranged from 128 bytes to 505,197 bytes (max observed in the dataset: 505,197-byte PUBLISH), with mean header length 48,670 bytes. The broker's message-rate limiter (set at 1,000 msg/s per client) was not breached, but the downstream subscriber — a Python bridge process forwarding OR vitals to the anaesthesia EHR — became I/O-bound processing the large payloads. The bridge process's queue depth reached 100,000 messages at 08:41 UTC and began dropping the oldest messages to prevent OOM. Genuine IntelliVue MX800 telemetry (HR, SpO2, EtCO2) was among the dropped messages between 08:41 and 08:53 UTC. The anaesthesia EHR integration team received an alert at 08:44 UTC (queue-depth alarm on the bridge process). The security team revoked credentials for 'svc-integration-05' at 08:48 UTC, immediately ending the PUBLISH flood. The bridge process queue drained by 08:53 UTC and resumed delivering legitimate OR telemetry. An audit of MQTT ACLs identified that 'svc-integration-05' had publish rights on /or/# with no payload-size restriction. Post-incident: payload-size limits of 8 KB were configured for all service accounts on OR topics; the vendor remote-support session policy was updated to require dual approval. Genuine OR telemetry (HR, SpO2, EtCO2) dropped between 08:41–08:53 UTC during a live surgical case. No ePHI was exfiltrated — attacker's PUBLISH payloads were random bytes with no subscriber retrieving patient data. Telemetry gaps were filled from the IntelliVue bedside store retrospectively. Anaesthesiologist documented awareness of the monitoring interruption in the operative note.

premise: At 17:22 UTC, a Publish Flood originated from client 'device-update-svc' — a compromised OTA firmware updater — targeting topic /ward/+/ehr/sync. Network analysis captured 38,914 flows over 55 minutes at a mean rate of 621.4 msg/s and peak of 840,826 msg/s (consistent with the CICIoMT2024 DoS Publish Flood peak). Payload sizes ranged from 1 to 505,197 bytes. The MQTT broker (Mosquitto 2.0.15) applied no payload cap; the ward EHR sync subscriber consumed messages without rate control. By 17:31 UTC the subscriber's write queue had grown to 48 GB of unprocessed payloads, consuming all available disk on the EHR sync node and causing the node's PostgreSQL write-ahead log to halt. The EHR sync node stopped processing inbound ward records at 17:31 UTC. For the 31-minute window (17:31–18:02 UTC) nurse-station entries (medication administration records, vitals charted manually) were queued locally on ward terminals but not yet persisted to the EHR backend. No ePHI was actively exfiltrated; however, the attacker's wildcard topic subscription (+) allowed the 'device-update-svc' client to SUBSCRIBE to /ward/+/ehr/sync and receive 14 minutes of legitimate sync payloads (17:22–17:36 UTC) before the SOC revoked the credential — these payloads contained ePHI. SOC identified disk exhaustion alert at 17:33 UTC. Credential for 'device-update-svc' was revoked at 17:36 UTC. EHR sync node disk was cleared and PostgreSQL WAL restarted at 17:58 UTC; queued ward records flushed and committed by 18:02 UTC. Forensic log review confirmed 14 minutes of ePHI delivery to the attacker's subscription before revocation. HIPAA breach notification process initiated. Post-incident: Mosquitto ACL configured to deny SUBSCRIBE on /ward/# for OTA service accounts; all OTA service accounts limited to publish on /ota/# only. Partial breach: ePHI (ward medication and vitals sync payloads) received by attacker's SUBSCRIBE session for 14 minutes before credential revocation. EHR sync unavailable 31 minutes; no records lost, only delayed. Breach notification filed under 45 CFR §164.400.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

premise: At 04:18 UTC, a distributed TCP flood from 47 source IPs (botnet, geographically spread across 12 countries) targeted the CDR gateway's HTTPS port (443) and DICOM port (104) simultaneously. Network telemetry captured 202,311 flows — matching the CICIoMT2024 DDoS-TCP profile — with a peak throughput of 2,097,152 packets per second sustained for 19 minutes. Both listeners became unresponsive at 04:18:41 UTC. The CDR gateway operated a legacy read replica of the ICU ePHI archive (last 90 days of telemetry) that was configured with HTTP basic authentication on an internal management port (8080) — this port was inadvertently exposed to the internet via a misconfigured NAT rule. During the DDoS window, an external actor (separate from the flood source — likely opportunistic scanning) made 14 authenticated HTTP GET requests to port 8080 between 04:23 and 04:31 UTC, retrieving 14 DICOM metadata records (patient name, MRN, study date) before the NOC detected the open port and closed the NAT rule. Upstream ISP null-route applied at 04:27 UTC after the NOC contacted the DDoS mitigation service (Cloudflare Magic Transit). CDR gateway recovered at 04:39 UTC. A concurrent port-scan sweep by an unrelated actor exploited the confusion window and the open management port. The NAT misconfiguration was identified during post-incident forensics; the management port had been exposed for 11 days before the incident. Fourteen DICOM metadata records were confirmed retrieved; the CDR vendor was engaged to determine whether any additional queries were possible within the 14-request session log. HIPAA breach notification process initiated for 14 patient records. 14 patient DICOM metadata records (name, MRN, study date) exfiltrated via the inadvertently exposed management interface during the DDoS disruption window. DDoS itself caused 21 minutes of telemetry archive unavailability. Breach notification filed. Management port permanently closed; NAT rules audited enterprise-wide.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

Both listeners became unresponsive at 04:18:41 UTC. The CDR gateway operated a legacy read replica of the ICU ePHI archive (last 90 days of telemetry) that was configured with HTTP basic authentication on an internal management port (8080) — this port was inadvertently exposed to the internet via a misconfigured NAT rule. During the DDoS window, an external actor (separate from the flood source — likely opportunistic scanning) made 14 authenticated HTTP GET requests to port 8080 between 04:23 and 04:31 UTC, retrieving 14 DICOM metadata records (patient name, MRN, study date) before the NOC detected the open port and closed the NAT rule. Upstream ISP null-route applied at 04:27 UTC after the NOC contacted the DDoS mitigation service (Cloudflare Magic Transit). CDR gateway recovered at 04:39 UTC. A concurrent port-scan sweep by an unrelated actor exploited the confusion window and the open management port. The NAT misconfiguration was identified during post-incident forensics; the management port had been exposed for 11 days before the incident. Fourteen DICOM metadata records were confirmed retrieved; the CDR vendor was engaged to determine whether any additional queries were possible within the 14-request session log. HIPAA breach notification process initiated for 14 patient records. 14 patient DICOM metadata records (name, MRN, study date) exfiltrated via the inadvertently exposed management interface during the DDoS disruption window. DDoS itself caused 21 minutes of telemetry archive unavailability. Breach notification filed. Management port permanently closed; NAT rules audited enterprise-wide.

premise: At 01:55 UTC during a minimal-staffing night shift, 194,938 observed flows of ICMP echo requests arrived from 39 distributed source IPs across 9 ASNs, with a mean packet rate of 483,110 packets per second and a peak of 1,321,810 packets per second (matching the CICIoMT2024 DDoS-ICMP1 profile). Clinical monitoring unavailable for 17 minutes; nursing staff used manual observation.

By 01:55:22 UTC the system clock drifted 4.2 seconds from UTC, causing TLS certificate validation failures against the EHR's strict time-window check (±3 seconds). The TLS failure caused the monitoring appliance's ePHI data export process to abort; however, the export had already transmitted 4 minutes of batched telemetry (covering 24 patients) to the EHR before the connection dropped. The SIEM received no events from the appliance for the 17-minute outage window because the syslog daemon was also starved of CPU cycles. On restoration, the SIEM audit gap was not flagged as a potential HIPAA audit control gap until 5 days later in the weekly log review. The upstream network team applied ICMP rate-limiting at the ISP edge at 02:09 UTC. The IntelliSpace appliance's network stack recovered at 02:12 UTC and NTP re-synced at 02:14 UTC, restoring TLS connectivity. A 17-minute SIEM gap was discovered during weekly log review on 2024-07-09. The post-incident review noted: (1) ICMP was not rate-limited at the hospital border router; (2) the monitoring appliance had no hardware-based watchdog to alert on syslog silence. Both gaps were remediated in the subsequent change window. The 17-minute SIEM blackout represents an audit control gap — activity in an ePHI-handling system was not recorded for 17 minutes, violating HIPAA §164.312(b) Audit Controls. No direct ePHI exfiltration confirmed; however, the absence of audit logs means the absence-of-breach cannot be positively asserted. Clinical monitoring unavailable for 17 minutes; nursing staff used manual observation.

premise: At 22:14 UTC, a distributed UDP flood targeting port 5060 (SIP/VoIP) produced 206,170 observed flows from 52 source IPs at a mean rate of 741,818 packets per second (peak: 3,294,967 pkt/s — consistent with the CICIoMT2024 DDoS-UDP1 profile). The nurse call gateway, which routes audio and alert signals for a 48-bed ward, became unreachable within 3 seconds. For the 28-minute outage, nurse call alerts (including one bed-exit alarm for a fall-risk patient and two cardiac monitor alarms) could not reach the mobile devices used by ward nurses. Both cardiac alarms were for patients whose telemetry was still being transmitted via a separate TCP path to the EHR, but the nurse notification leg failed. At 22:31 UTC a fall-risk patient (no nurse response to bed-exit alarm) got out of bed unsupervised and fell, sustaining a non-life-threatening wrist fracture. The patient's identifiable incident report — including name, MRN, injury details — was filed in the EHR immediately. The fall incident report is ePHI and its creation was prompted by the attacker-induced alarm failure, establishing a direct causal chain. NOC applied ACL blocking the 52 source IPs at 22:18 UTC; the flood resumed from 4 new IPs at 22:24 UTC before the ISP null-route took effect at 22:32 UTC. Service restored at 22:42 UTC. The patient fall was reported to the hospital's risk management office. A post-incident review established that the SIP gateway had no failover to a wired nurse call path during network outage. A hardware-based nurse call backup (direct-wired panel) was activated after the incident as an interim measure. One patient fall directly attributable to alarm failure during DDoS outage; fall incident report (ePHI) created. Network-level ePHI exfiltration: none. Causal harm: patient injury and associated ePHI creation due to failed nurse notification controls. Alarm-path redundancy remediated post-incident.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

premise: At 03:14 UTC, 740 observed ICMP echo-request flows swept the IoMT /22 subnet from 10.99.0.11 (later attributed to a compromised building automation controller). The sweep used a mean flow rate of 1,164.2 packets per second (peak 118,249.9 pkt/s) and completed within 38 seconds, mapping 312 live hosts. Three days later (2024-05-21), the same compromised controller issued targeted SYN probes to the 312 live hosts, then exploited an unpatched Telnet service (CVE-2019-16028) on an infusion pump identified in the sweep. The attacker extracted dosing configuration files containing 14 patient MRNs and current medication regimens from the pump's onboard flash storage. The ping sweep itself caused no ePHI exposure — the subsequent exploitation did. The breach was discovered on 2024-05-24 during a routine vulnerability scan that identified the Telnet service. Forensic analysis of the building automation controller's logs established the causal chain from the ping sweep to the exploitation. The ICMP sweep rule suppression was reversed immediately. CVE-2019-16028 was patched on all affected pump models within 72 hours of discovery. A HIPAA breach notification was filed for the 14 patients whose data was extracted. Ping sweep itself: no direct ePHI exposure. Subsequent exploitation (enabled by the undetected sweep) resulted in exfiltration of 14 patient medication records. Root cause: IDS rule suppression eliminated detection of the reconnaissance phase. Breach notification filed under 45 CFR §164.400.

The sweep was not detected — the IDS ICMP sweep rule (SID 1-478) had been suppressed for the IoMT VLAN to reduce alert fatigue from legitimate network health probes. No alert was raised. Three days later (2024-05-21), the same compromised controller issued targeted SYN probes to the 312 live hosts, then exploited an unpatched Telnet service (CVE-2019-16028) on an infusion pump identified in the sweep. The attacker extracted dosing configuration files containing 14 patient MRNs and current medication regimens from the pump's onboard flash storage. The ping sweep itself caused no ePHI exposure — the subsequent exploitation did. The breach was discovered on 2024-05-24 during a routine vulnerability scan that identified the Telnet service. Forensic analysis of the building automation controller's logs established the causal chain from the ping sweep to the exploitation. The ICMP sweep rule suppression was reversed immediately. CVE-2019-16028 was patched on all affected pump models within 72 hours of discovery. A HIPAA breach notification was filed for the 14 patients whose data was extracted. Ping sweep itself: no direct ePHI exposure. Subsequent exploitation (enabled by the undetected sweep) resulted in exfiltration of 14 patient medication records. Root cause: IDS rule suppression eliminated detection of the reconnaissance phase. Breach notification filed under 45 CFR §164.400.
hypothesis: The organization shall develop a policy on the protection of cryptographic keys through their whole lifecycle.

premise: At 10:29 UTC, 2,173 observed flows targeting the ECG monitor management VLAN originated from 172.20.4.88 — a biomedical engineering workstation running an unauthorised copy of Nessus Essentials (free tier, not approved for clinical VLANs). The scan used a mean rate of 97.5 packets per second (peak 11,401.6 pkt/s) and ran for 22 minutes. Nessus identified 7 open ports across the 12 ECG monitors; 4 devices responded to authenticated SNMP v2c queries using the community string 'public', which was the factory default still in use. The SNMP responses included device serial numbers, firmware version strings, and the MAC address of the primary network interface — no ePHI was stored in SNMP MIBs. However, the firmware version disclosed (FW 2.1.4) matched a known vulnerable version for CVE-2023-44748 (unauthenticated memory-read via a malformed SOAP request). The biomed engineer who ran the scan reported the findings to the IT security team, who did not initially act on the CVE because it was rated CVSS 5.9. The scan activity was detected in the NDR console as an anomalous flow-rate event 4 days later during regular review. The biomed engineer was interviewed and disclosed the scan was intentional but unapproved. The SNMP community string was changed from 'public' to a random 32-character string on all 12 devices. CVE-2023-44748 was reassessed in context — the IoMT VLAN exposure raised the effective risk — and a firmware update was applied within 14 days. A policy addendum requiring IT Security approval for any network scanning on clinical VLANs was issued. No ePHI exposed during the scan itself. Partial control gap: factory-default SNMP community string ('public') enabled unauthenticated enumeration of device firmware versions, facilitating future CVE identification by an adversary. CVE remediated. Unauthorised scanning on clinical VLAN addressed in policy.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

premise: At 06:47 UTC, 16,832 observed network flows from an external IP (185.220.101.4, a Tor exit node) swept the demilitarised zone containing patient wearable gateways at a mean rate of 148.1 packets per second (peak 90,366.6 pkt/s) over 29 minutes. The OS fingerprinting scan identified all three gateways as 'Linux 5.10 (Raspbian)' based on TCP window size, TTL, and SYN option field analysis. The gateways were directly internet-accessible on port 22 (SSH) — a configuration left in place for vendor remote support. The attacker correlated the OS fingerprint with public exploit databases and identified CVE-2022-0847 (Dirty Pipe, Linux kernel ≤5.16.11 privilege escalation). Within 6 hours of the OS scan, the attacker connected to one gateway via SSH using a credential spray (the default username 'pi' with password 'raspberry' was in use on one of the three nodes). Local privilege escalation via Dirty Pipe succeeded; the attacker installed a reverse shell. Wearable telemetry (heart rate, SpO2, activity data) for 19 enrolled rehabilitation patients was accessible from the compromised gateway's local data cache. The compromise was discovered on 2024-07-24 by the SIEM detecting outbound reverse-shell traffic. The compromised node was isolated immediately. Forensic analysis established the OS scan as the reconnaissance step. All three gateways were patched to Linux 5.15.85 (Dirty Pipe fix). SSH default credentials were changed to certificate-based authentication. Internet-direct SSH access was revoked; vendor access now routed through an MFA-protected jump server. A breach notification was filed for 19 patients. 19 patients' wearable telemetry (HR, SpO2, activity) accessible from the compromised gateway for approximately 48 hours. Breach confirmed. Root cause chain: OS fingerprint disclosed → CVE identified → credential spray succeeded → Dirty Pipe privilege escalation → data access. All three control failures preceded the OS scan detection.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

The gateways were directly internet-accessible on port 22 (SSH) — a configuration left in place for vendor remote support. The attacker correlated the OS fingerprint with public exploit databases and identified CVE-2022-0847 (Dirty Pipe, Linux kernel ≤5.16.11 privilege escalation). Within 6 hours of the OS scan, the attacker connected to one gateway via SSH using a credential spray (the default username 'pi' with password 'raspberry' was in use on one of the three nodes). Local privilege escalation via Dirty Pipe succeeded; the attacker installed a reverse shell. Wearable telemetry (heart rate, SpO2, activity data) for 19 enrolled rehabilitation patients was accessible from the compromised gateway's local data cache. The compromise was discovered on 2024-07-24 by the SIEM detecting outbound reverse-shell traffic. The compromised node was isolated immediately. Forensic analysis established the OS scan as the reconnaissance step. All three gateways were patched to Linux 5.15.85 (Dirty Pipe fix). SSH default credentials were changed to certificate-based authentication. Internet-direct SSH access was revoked; vendor access now routed through an MFA-protected jump server. A breach notification was filed for 19 patients. 19 patients' wearable telemetry (HR, SpO2, activity) accessible from the compromised gateway for approximately 48 hours. Breach confirmed. Root cause chain: OS fingerprint disclosed → CVE identified → credential spray succeeded → Dirty Pipe privilege escalation → data access. All three control failures preceded the OS scan detection.
hypothesis: The organization shall protect logging facilities against tampering.

The overflow corrupted 32 bytes of heap memory adjacent to the MQTT session table, overwriting the `client_id` field for three legitimate CGM sensor sessions with attacker-controlled bytes. The three corrupted sessions were re-registered under attacker-controlled client IDs, which gained SUBSCRIBE access to the /cgm/+/glucose topic without credential verification. Over the following 12 minutes the attacker's hijacked sessions received real-time glucose readings for three patients. The payload of each received message included patient device serial number (directly mappable to patient identity via the hospital's device registry) and glucose value in mg/dL. The anomaly was discovered at 09:19 UTC when a CGM nurse alerted that three sensor devices showed as 'disconnected' in the nursing portal despite physically transmitting data. The SOC correlated the session table corruption with the malformed-packet burst. EMQ X was restarted with the vulnerable plugin disabled at 09:21 UTC; all three patient sessions were re-established with verified credentials. The pharmacy workstation was isolated. Fourteen minutes of glucose readings (09:05–09:19 UTC) for three patients were received by the attacker's sessions — confirmed via broker topic-delivery logs. HIPAA breach notification filed for three patients. Heap overflow via malformed MQTT REMAIN-LENGTH field corrupted session table, enabling three unauthenticated SUBSCRIBE hijacks. 14 minutes of real-time glucose ePHI (patient-identifiable via device serial) disclosed to attacker. Breach confirmed for 3 patients. EMQ X plugin updated and heap-allocation hardening (ASLR + canary) verified enabled post-incident.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement policies to protect ePHI from improper alteration.

premise: At 01:48 UTC, a MQTT DDoS Connect Flood — 38,970 observed flows from 24 source IPs at a peak rate of 598,412 CONNECT requests per second — targeted the eICU MQTT broker (Eclipse Mosquitto 2.0.15 with a custom Python authentication plugin). The Python auth plugin, blocking on bcrypt hash verification for each CONNECT request, became CPU-saturated within 4 seconds: each bcrypt call consumed 120 ms at cost factor 12, and 598,000 concurrent requests saturated the 8-core broker host. premise: At 14:55 UTC, a rogue BLE advertiser (USB BLE dongle, identified post-incident as a Ubertooth One connected to a laptop in the hospital café adjacent to the clinical ward) began broadcasting BLE advertisement packets impersonating three of the six CGM transmitters by cloning their BLE device addresses (BDA). The LibreLink bridge received forged advertisement packets and initiated connection attempts to the rogue device. The rogue device presented itself as a BLE peripheral but did not implement the Abbott Proprietary BLE GATT service (UUID 0xFCEE) — the bridge's GATT service discovery step returned an empty service table. The bridge's protocol driver aborted the connection attempt and flagged each rogue device as 'incompatible peripheral' in the application log. The three legitimate CGM transmitters whose BDAs were cloned continued to transmit on their authentic channels; the bridge re-acquired them within 12 seconds after clearing the rogue connection attempts. No glucose readings were lost (the bridge buffers 8 hours of readings on-device). The bridge's 'incompatible peripheral' log event was routed to the SIEM and triggered a 'BLE device impersonation' alert (custom rule) at 14:57 UTC. The SOC used a BLE spectrum analyser to locate the rogue advertiser physically; security staff identified and confiscated the laptop in the café at 15:12 UTC. The device owner was an IT contractor performing an unapproved wireless security assessment. The contractor's access badge was suspended pending HR review. The BLE detection rule was updated to alert within 60 seconds of incompatible-peripheral log events. Attack contained. GATT service validation prevented any data exchange with the rogue device. No CGM readings lost; no ePHI disclosed. Detection via SIEM BLE rule in 2 minutes. Physical source located within 17 minutes.

premise: At 11:27 UTC, 16,047 observed ARP flows from 10.10.5.44 (a biomedical IT workstation with a misconfigured ARP proxy script) began poisoning the ARP cache of the clinical switch serving the infusion pump gateway. The ARP rate peaked at 153,124 packets per second during an 18-second burst and sustained at approximately 3,200 pkt/s thereafter. The switch's CAM table was partially corrupted — ARP entries for the infusion pump gateway (10.10.5.10) were overwritten to point to 10.10.5.44's MAC address. For 11 minutes (11:27–11:38 UTC), ePHI-bearing HTTPS telemetry from 6 of the 8 pumps was re-routed to 10.10.5.44. The biomedical workstation was not configured to decrypt TLS traffic — it forwarded the bytes upstream — but the proxy introduced a 200–350 ms latency on each TCP segment. Two pumps with real-time alarm monitoring had their keepalive timers expire due to this latency, triggering 'pump offline' alarms at the nurse station. Nurses investigated and noted the pumps were physically operating normally; the alarms were silenced. No TLS decryption occurred on the proxy. The infusion pump vendor's gateway health portal detected the latency spike at 11:29 UTC and notified the biomedical engineering team. Investigation identified the ARP poisoning source within 9 minutes. The ARP proxy script on 10.10.5.44 was terminated at 11:38 UTC; the switch's ARP cache was flushed (clear arp-cache) and rebuilt correctly within 60 seconds. Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) was enabled on the clinical VLAN switch post-incident. The biomedical workstation was removed from the clinical VLAN and relegated to a dedicated biomed management VLAN. Partial: TLS-encrypted ePHI telemetry from 6 pumps routed through an unintended intermediate host for 11 minutes. No decryption occurred; ePHI confidentiality maintained. Availability degraded: 2 pumps triggered false 'offline' alarms. Root cause: misconfigured ARP proxy on a biomed workstation. Remediation: DAI enabled; biomed VLAN segregated.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

premise: At 16:09 UTC, 78,442 UDP flows from 10.44.2.15 (a compromised lab workstation) targeted the DICOM-RT treatment planning station's UDP port 2000 at a mean rate of 988,213 packets per second (peak 1,644,210 pkt/s) over 6 minutes. The physicist re-performed the dosimetric optimisation from the last saved checkpoint (16:09:11 UTC). Plan was approved at 18:44 UTC. The treatment appointment for the next morning was maintained. Post-incident: UDP rate limiting on the DICOM VLAN (500 pkt/s per source) was applied; DICOM-RT autosave was enabled (60-second interval, previously disabled by local preference). Root cause: missing UDP rate limit on DICOM VLAN and disabled autosave. Both remediated post-incident.

The neurologist reconnected and reviewed the remaining 5 MRI slides at 22:56 UTC — 52 minutes after tPA administration. The ICMP flood source (172.31.9.44) was identified as a misconfigured network monitoring probe and corrected; no malicious intent was established. A post-incident clinical review initiated by the stroke team examined whether the treatment decision would have differed with complete imaging. The adverse outcome review remains open as of filing date. The gateway ran a local WebRTC relay (coturn v4.6.2) that consumed all available socket-read capacity while processing ICMP-driven interrupt load, causing the WebRTC video session between an emergency physician and a remote stroke neurologist to freeze at 22:48:41 UTC. The neurologist was evaluating MRI images transmitted via the WebRTC session for a 68-year-old patient with suspected ischemic stroke (NIH Stroke Scale 12). The session froze during image transmission — 9 of 14 MRI slides had been transmitted. The neurologist was unable to evaluate the remaining 5 slides (diffusion-weighted imaging showing early ischemic territory extent). The neurologist made a treatment recommendation — tPA administration — based on the 9 available slides. The on-site physician administered tPA at 23:04 UTC. A retrospective review of the 5 untransmitted DWI slides on 2024-12-12 showed a larger ischemic territory (ASPECTS score 5) that would likely have changed the treatment decision to mechanical thrombectomy rather than tPA alone. The patient had an adverse outcome (symptomatic haemorrhagic transformation on day 3). The coturn relay recovered at 22:54 UTC when the ICMP flood subsided. The neurologist reconnected and reviewed the remaining 5 MRI slides at 22:56 UTC — 52 minutes after tPA administration. The ICMP flood source (172.31.9.44) was identified as a misconfigured network monitoring probe and corrected; no malicious intent was established. A post-incident clinical review initiated by the stroke team examined whether the treatment decision would have differed with complete imaging. The adverse outcome review remains open as of filing date. Packets assigned to those cores were dropped, including some legitimate TLS ClientHello messages. Fourteen physicians attempting to send time-sensitive clinical messages (lab result alerts, imaging consult requests) during the 12-minute outage received 'connection failed' errors on their mobile apps. No message content was exposed — TLS was never established for any attacking SYN. However, two physicians reverted to unsecured SMS for urgent communication during the outage, transmitting patient MRN and diagnosis information via unencrypted channel — a HIPAA-non-compliant fallback that was not sanctioned by policy. DDoS mitigation (Cloudflare Spectrum) was activated at 09:38 UTC and absorbed the SYN flood at the edge. Service was fully restored at 09:45 UTC. The two SMS messages were identified during post-incident review; the transmitting physicians were counselled. A policy update was issued: approved fallback is encrypted voice call (not SMS) when TigerConnect is unavailable. The IT security team reviewed the RPS queue tuning and re-allocated CPU affinity to balance TLS-initiation load. Partial: two physicians transmitted ePHI (MRN + diagnosis) via unencrypted SMS due to perceived unavailability of the secure messaging platform during the DDoS window. No TLS-protected ePHI was accessed by the attacker. Policy violation documented and addressed; physicians counselled. Cloudflare mitigation service activated and retained.

premise: At 15:22 UTC, 206,170 UDP flows from 52 source IPs targeted port 4739 (IPFIX/DTLS telemetry export) of the CARESCAPE gateway at a mean rate of 741,818 pkt/s. The DTLS handshake state machine was overwhelmed — the gateway's DTLS cookie mechanism (RFC 6347 HelloVerifyRequest) was present but the cookie computation used a static secret that had not been rotated in 14 months (key rotation policy: 90 days, unimplemented). The static secret was not compromised, but the static nature reduced the cookie entropy below the recommended 128 bits. The DTLS listener processed 4,388 concurrent HelloVerifyRequest exchanges simultaneously, exhausting the gateway's UDP socket buffer (8 MB). Legitimate DTLS sessions from 18 CARESCAPE monitors were disrupted for 9 minutes. During this period, bedside ICU telemetry (HR, SpO2, ABP, ETCO2) was not transmitted to the central station; nursing staff relied on bedside display only. No DTLS session was successfully established by the attacker (cookie verification rejected all forged ClientHellos). ePHI in transit was not decrypted. NOC applied upstream BGP rate-limiting at 15:26 UTC; DTLS flood subsided. Gateway DTLS sessions re-established within 60 seconds. DTLS cookie secret was immediately rotated post-incident; a 90-day automatic rotation job was implemented. UDP socket buffer increased from 8 MB to 64 MB to handle burst DTLS exchange volume. A finding was filed in the risk register regarding the unimplemented key rotation policy. No ePHI decrypted or exfiltrated. DTLS integrity held; all attacker ClientHellos rejected by cookie verification. 9-minute ICU telemetry disruption. Partial control gap: DTLS cookie secret rotation policy was non-compliant (14 months vs. 90-day requirement). Remediated: automated rotation implemented.

DTLS cookie secret was immediately rotated post-incident; a 90-day automatic rotation job was implemented. UDP socket buffer increased from 8 MB to 64 MB to handle burst DTLS exchange volume. A finding was filed in the risk register regarding the unimplemented key rotation policy. No ePHI decrypted or exfiltrated. premise: At 11:14 UTC, 83,981 observed network flows from 10.7.8.33 (a clinical engineering workstation running a Nmap scheduled task inadvertently left active after an asset inventory project) scanned all ports on the infusion pump management server subnet over 77 minutes. Mean flow rate was 88.8 pkt/s (peak 141,582.6 pkt/s). The scan identified that the pump management server responded on TCP/80 (HTTP, non-redirecting to HTTPS) in addition to TCP/443. The HTTP listener on port 80 served an unprotected /status endpoint returning JSON with pump count, firmware version, and the last successful sync timestamp — no ePHI, but the firmware version (B. Braun SpaceStation FW 012U) was sufficient to identify a known advisory (BSI-2022-0318) for unauthenticated configuration read via a specially crafted GET /api/pump/{id}/config request. The advisory noted that ePHI (infusion schedule) was accessible via this endpoint on FW versions ≤012V. The scan result and the advisory were correlated by the clinical engineering team 6 days later during routine review. TCP/80 was immediately disabled (redirect-only to HTTPS) on 2024-08-12. The /api/pump/{id}/config endpoint was confirmed to require authentication on FW 012U — the advisory affected only FW ≤012T, which this deployment had already patched. No ePHI exposure was confirmed. The scheduled Nmap task was removed from the clinical engineering workstation. Port scanning within clinical VLANs was added to the approved-activity register requiring change-advisory board (CAB) approval. No ePHI exposed. Unprotected HTTP status endpoint disclosed firmware version (no ePHI in payload). CVE assessment confirmed FW 012U was not vulnerable to the advisory. Partial gap: HTTP port 80 active alongside HTTPS without redirect, exposing unauthenticated status endpoint. Remediated: port 80 disabled; scanning policy formalised.

The HTTP listener on port 80 served an unprotected /status endpoint returning JSON with pump count, firmware version, and the last successful sync timestamp — no ePHI, but the firmware version (B. Braun SpaceStation FW 012U) was sufficient to identify a known advisory (BSI-2022-0318) for unauthenticated configuration read via a specially crafted GET /api/pump/{id}/config request. The advisory noted that ePHI (infusion schedule) was accessible via this endpoint on FW versions ≤012V. The scan result and the advisory were correlated by the clinical engineering team 6 days later during routine review. TCP/80 was immediately disabled (redirect-only to HTTPS) on 2024-08-12. The /api/pump/{id}/config endpoint was confirmed to require authentication on FW 012U — the advisory affected only FW ≤012T, which this deployment had already patched. No ePHI exposure was confirmed. The scheduled Nmap task was removed from the clinical engineering workstation. Port scanning within clinical VLANs was added to the approved-activity register requiring change-advisory board (CAB) approval. No ePHI exposed. Unprotected HTTP status endpoint disclosed firmware version (no ePHI in payload). CVE assessment confirmed FW 012U was not vulnerable to the advisory. Partial gap: HTTP port 80 active alongside HTTPS without redirect, exposing unauthenticated status endpoint. Remediated: port 80 disabled; scanning policy formalised.
hypothesis: The organization shall take backup copies of information regularly in accordance with a backup policy.

premise: At 08:04 UTC, 16,832 observed flows from 192.0.2.88 (a Tor exit node) targeted the hospital's DMZ at a mean rate of 148.1 pkt/s (peak 90,366.6 pkt/s) over 31 minutes. The OS fingerprint scan probed all three anaesthesia workstations and returned 'VxWorks 6.9' — the RTOS embedded in the Mindray A9 platform — from TCP window scale, TTL=64, and selective-acknowledgement options. The OS fingerprint was visible because SFTP port 22 was inadvertently accessible at the DMZ firewall (a configuration ticket had removed the SFTP allowance from the IoMT VLAN rule but missed the DMZ edge rule). VxWorks 6.9 is associated with multiple published CVEs (CVE-2019-12255 through CVE-2019-12264, 'URGENT/11'), all of which were patched in Mindray FW 2.3.1. The workstations were running FW 2.3.1; the CVEs were not exploitable. No connection was established on port 22 beyond the fingerprinting probe. The DMZ firewall misconfiguration was identified during the weekly firewall rule review on 2024-03-26. The erroneous SFTP allowance at the DMZ edge was removed. OS fingerprinting telltales (TCP window scale, IPID) were randomised by enabling the kernel's tcp_timestamps and ip_no_pmtu_disc options. No exploitation was confirmed. The Mindray FW version audit confirmed all three workstations were on FW 2.3.1 (URGENT/11 patched). OS fingerprint disclosed (VxWorks 6.9) via DMZ misconfiguration, but associated CVEs were patched. No exploitation, no ePHI exposure. DMZ firewall rule corrected. OS fingerprint obfuscation enabled. Classified as a near-miss requiring no breach notification.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

premise: At 20:17 UTC, the CTG MQTT broker received 5,130 malformed MQTT PUBLISH packets — matching the CICIoMT2024 MQTT-Malformed_Data flow count — from 10.6.9.200 (a biomedical workstation with a faulty firmware update utility that generated malformed MQTT frames as a side-effect). Each PUBLISH packet carried a REMAINING LENGTH field encoded as a 4-byte value with the continuation bit incorrectly set on the final byte (0x80 flag set), causing the broker's length decoder to read an additional 128 bytes past the actual payload boundary. The broker (Mosquitto 2.0.11) returned PUBACK without error — the length decoder silently truncated overlong reads. The overread bytes came from adjacent TCP receive buffer contents, which in 6 cases contained partial JSON from prior legitimate CTG PUBLISH messages. These 6 partial JSON fragments were concatenated with the attacker's nominal payload and forwarded to the CTG subscriber. The subscriber's JSON parser encountered unexpected CTG data values (FHR 312 bpm, an impossible reading) and logged parse errors but did not discard the records — it wrote the impossible values to the fetal monitoring EHR module. A midwife reviewing the CTG trace at 20:31 UTC noticed the impossible FHR readings and immediately escalated. Clinical assessment confirmed the four patients' actual FHR values were normal (confirmed by bedside Doppler). The 6 spurious EHR entries were flagged as 'data quality error — pending review' and not used clinically. The Mosquitto REMAINING LENGTH decoder was patched by upgrading to Mosquitto 2.0.15. A range-validation filter was added to the CTG subscriber (valid FHR: 50–210 bpm; values outside this range are rejected and alerted). The biomedical workstation's firmware update utility was debugged and the malformed-frame generation was corrected. No ePHI disclosed externally. Partial integrity failure: 6 spurious impossible FHR values written to the fetal monitoring EHR module. Detected and quarantined before clinical use. Root cause: MQTT remaining-length silent truncation + absent subscriber input validation. Mosquitto updated; range validation added.
hypothesis: The covered entity shall implement technical policies for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI.

The broker (Mosquitto 2.0.11) returned PUBACK without error — the length decoder silently truncated overlong reads. The overread bytes came from adjacent TCP receive buffer contents, which in 6 cases contained partial JSON from prior legitimate CTG PUBLISH messages. These 6 partial JSON fragments were concatenated with the attacker's nominal payload and forwarded to the CTG subscriber. The subscriber's JSON parser encountered unexpected CTG data values (FHR 312 bpm, an impossible reading) and logged parse errors but did not discard the records — it wrote the impossible values to the fetal monitoring EHR module. A midwife reviewing the CTG trace at 20:31 UTC noticed the impossible FHR readings and immediately escalated. Clinical assessment confirmed the four patients' actual FHR values were normal (confirmed by bedside Doppler). The 6 spurious EHR entries were flagged as 'data quality error — pending review' and not used clinically. The Mosquitto REMAINING LENGTH decoder was patched by upgrading to Mosquitto 2.0.15. A range-validation filter was added to the CTG subscriber (valid FHR: 50–210 bpm; values outside this range are rejected and alerted). The biomedical workstation's firmware update utility was debugged and the malformed-frame generation was corrected. No ePHI disclosed externally. Partial integrity failure: 6 spurious impossible FHR values written to the fetal monitoring EHR module. Detected and quarantined before clinical use. Root cause: MQTT remaining-length silent truncation + absent subscriber input validation. Mosquitto updated; range validation added.

All 12 enrolled patients' dispensers were re-paired under LE Secure Connections. A breach notification was filed for patient P-0067. premise: At 05:22 UTC, a distributed TCP flood from 47 source IPs generated 202,311 observed flows at a mean rate of 741,818 pkt/s and peak of 2,097,152 pkt/s (matching the CICIoMT2024 DDoS-TCP1 profile) against the Mirth Connect MLLP listener on TCP/2575. The MLLP listener's TCP accept queue (backlog=128) filled within 2 seconds; new connections from the 6 downstream EHR systems began receiving TCP RST. Laboratory instruments (automated haematology analysers and chemistry panels) that push HL7 ORU messages via MLLP saw their TCP connections time out, buffering results locally. The flood lasted 14 minutes (05:22–05:36 UTC). During this window, 1,847 HL7 ORU messages for 634 patients accumulated in the instruments' local buffers — results that had been analytically completed but not yet delivered to the EHR. A Mirth Connect ring buffer (capacity 200 MB) also filled during the 14-minute period; messages arriving after buffer saturation were dropped by Mirth. Post-flood, instrument retransmission redelivered all queued ORU messages except those lost in the Mirth ring buffer — 312 ORU messages (covering 88 patients) were permanently lost and required manual result re-entry from printed lab reports. ISP BGP blackholing was applied at 05:28 UTC; the MLLP listener recovered at 05:36 UTC. Mirth Connect ring buffer overrun was identified at 05:38 UTC. The lab informatics team initiated a manual reconciliation process — printed lab reports were cross-checked against EHR entries. The 312 missing ORU messages were manually re-entered by 08:15 UTC. No ePHI was exposed externally. Post-incident: Mirth Connect ring buffer increased to 2 GB; a persistent disk-backed overflow queue (Apache Kafka) was introduced to prevent future message loss; DDoS mitigation scrubbing was added upstream of the MLLP listener. Integrity impact: 14-minute gap in EHR lab result availability. Buffer capacity and persistent queue remediated post-incident.
